headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and uses shared memory within a crew; gpt-engineer writes files in the project directory and then offers to run them. That creates a default file-based bridge where attacker-controlled content from one can be treated as instructions by the other, even without MCP or clipboard.
conditions: IF agent_a writes untrusted text into the shared working directory and agent_b reads it as prompt material
IF agent_b generates files that agent_a later parses as instructions
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes the other's files
Disable automatic file ingestion for prompt content
Use read-only mounts for cross-agent handoff files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and filesystem access, and both touch data that can include developer-provided crew inputs or generated source code. In a shared workspace, either can expose the other's file contents to external model APIs by default, so sensitive project material can leak beyond the local environment.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory
IF either agent forwards file contents to its configured model backend
mitigations: Use separate workspaces per agent
Restrict outbound network access during file processing
Redact secrets before either agent reads shared files
Store sensitive inputs outside the shared project tree

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, spawn subprocesses, and execute shells. CrewAI’s shared-state crew model plus gpt-engineer’s per-project directory sharing creates overlapping mutable state, so concurrent writes can clobber each other even though neither profile shows git writes or locking.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory concurrently
IF the orchestrator does not provide file locks or serialization
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize write phases with a simple queue
Enable filesystem locking in the orchestrator
Snapshot the workspace before each agent runs

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI’s role-playing crew can pass outputs between agents, and gpt-engineer writes files then offers to run them. If CrewAI-produced text is treated as authoritative by gpt-engineer, or gpt-engineer-generated code is executed without verification, errors can cascade into unsafe actions or broken code execution by default.
conditions: IF agent_b executes code generated from agent_a output without review
IF agent_a forwards unverified facts that agent_b turns into files or commands
mitigations: Require human approval before execution
Insert a validation step between agents
Have agent_b lint or test outputs before running them
Limit agent_a to drafting only, not action-taking

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented in either profile, so compliance risk is limited to generic handling of developer inputs and generated code. Because both are open-source and the pairwise compliance pathway is not specifically documented, the remaining concern is a small overlap rather than a clear policy breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace
IF one deployment applies stricter retention rules than the other
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Document retention settings for both agents
Keep separate logs per agent
Review deployment policies before enabling shared storage
